have seen Calmann-Levy’s SIMUIACRAS, which is an especially lovely edition— the contrast to the original U.S. edition by Ace is appalling. I even wrote Calmann-Levy to thank them. 

We arrive now at the hard questions: “What your repetitive utilization of the simulacra theme means to you?” This is why I suggest you read my Vancou­ ver speech, because it is subtided _The Authentic Human versus the Reflex Machine_ (the tide is, “The Human and the Android”). I spent as many months writing the speech as I do writing a novel, and I tried to express in clear terms my feel­ ing that we have two types of people, one authentic, the other a cold and calculat­ ing “machine” (these are metaphors of course, “machine and android,” etc). In my speech I tried to define the authentic human and I know you will forgive me if I do not do it again here but beg off, directing you to the Vancouver speech. There are so many factors contained and expressed in the authentic human, and even the “android” or “simulacrum” are complex—the same way a color TV cir­ cuit is complex. Shortly after giving my speech in Vancouver, both at the conven­ tion and at the University of British Columbia, I decided to stay on in Canada and become a citizen. A technical qualification barred me, however, and I had to return to the U.S. But while I was there I spent a month in a heroin rehabilita­ tion center, and I saw, all around me, the “android” personality with its cold opaque eyes that reflected nothing .... I saw in the truest sense the dreadful thing I had been writing about. I think the basic issues involved (as in drug addiction) are Being versus Non-Being. Heroin suffocates the brain; it cuts down and even out all body signals. These people did not want body signals, and their eyes showed it; they did not want to live or be in any ontological sense. Freud once said that in each of us there is Eros (life) and Thanos (death). I think he was right. In many people the Eros drive wanes, and rising to fill the vacuum is the need for slow death. It is not so much that these people _want_ to die; actually they want nothing. They simply have lost the zest, the enthusiasm, the interest, for and about life; they have no curiosity, no humor ... I must admit, myself, to hav­ ing episodes when the Thanos drive begins to overpower the Eros. Several times I’ either tried to kill myself or been so depressed that had no one intervened, I would have. Is this not, then, the psychological motive for my writing about these two types? “Two hearts burn in my breast,” Goethe has Faust say, and surely this is true (I guess he said ‘Seele,’ which is soul). Yes, of course it is soul. The heart is warm and beats will forgiveness and tenderness for oneself and one’s fellow—for all man, for the animals equally. But the simulacrum person­ look into his eyes. He shows no caritas, no concern. Psychiatrically, he has been given the name “Schizoid,” which is a person who tries to think his way through life rather than feel. We, who are authentic, _feel_ and depend on those feelings. But once, long ago, when I was between 16 and 28, I was a thinking, cold, ratio­ nal, practical type. Something changed me. So I suppose in answer to your ques­ tion, I am obsessed with this question because even now, as recendy as last month, my Eros drive waned, and I considered killing myself.
